claims.text: The target particles are sub-10 nm, near-equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles with an initially single-phase, chemically homogeneous solid solution.
Premelting onset in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles is governed by copper segregation to the particle surface.
Copper has a relatively lower melting point than the other relevant alloy constituents.
Copper has relatively lower cohesive energy than the other relevant alloy constituents.
Copper atoms have higher surface diffusivity in these nanoparticles.
Differences in atomic properties enable copper atoms to migrate toward and accumulate at the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Copper enrichment at the surface reduces the local melting barrier.
The copper-enriched surface region becomes disordered and forms a quasi-molten premelting layer.
The quasi-molten surface layer acts as a precursor to complete nanoparticle melting.
Surface disordering begins below the bulk melting temperature.
Premelting will be accompanied by a copper-enriched surface layer observable using EDS mapping and high-resolution imaging.
Partial substitution of copper by a higher-melting element such as molybdenum will suppress copper segregation.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit surface premelting at a lower temperature than nanoparticles in which copper is partially replaced by molybdenum.
Chemically homogeneous nanoparticles lacking significant differential surface diffusivity should melt more uniformly and without a distinct copper-driven premelting step.
The proposed mechanism applies to sub-10 nm, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles under high vacuum or inert atmosphere.
Larger particle size, oxidizing conditions, or initial chemical inhomogeneity may change the premelting mechanism.
